units.text:
Post Graduate
AcademicWriting

Definitions and Course Overview


• Academic writing, with a few exceptions, is essay writing
 based on research.
• An essay is an attempt to prove a thesis with evidence.
• Evidence, there will be more on what is good and bad
 evidence later, is verifiable facts, examples and the like.
• Academic writing is judged by the quality of your
 evidence and how effectively your interpretation of the
 evidence relates to your thesis.

Continued


• This course will start with some basic principles of effective
 writing in English. These are being concise, clear and concrete.
• This will be followed by the structure of an effective essay—
 introduction, thesis, body (this includes understanding how to
 handle evidence) and conclusions.
• Inherent in discussing the nature of essays is the writing
 process and revision.
• We will read and discuss both good and flawed essays and you
 will write a few.

On Being Concise


• Concise means conveying your meaning in as few words
 as possible.
• Avoid wasting time on preliminaries or transitions.
 Preliminaries, or introductory comments, when you are
 moving from one topic to another in the body of your
 paper, are generally unnecessary. Also, keep your
 transitions short and to the point. Transition words should
 really appear at the beginning or the end of a paragraph;
 they should rarely appear in the middle of a paragraph.

Concise Cont’d



• Avoid empty words, phrases and sentences. An empty use
 of words simply means that the word, phrase or sentence
 adds no meaning to what you are trying to write. Every
 word, with a few exceptions, in your sentences should be
 directly connected to the subject, verb or objects. If it is
 not, then it probably is an empty word or phrase.

More on Empty Words


• Some other common empty phrases that add no meaning to
 your sentences:
• All things considered
• As far as I am concerned
• For all intents and purposes
• In a manner of speaking
• Last but not least
• More or less
• The two most common empty sentences are “This is a
 controversial topic.” and “Everyone has a right to their own opinion.”

Wordiness


• Avoid being wordy. Wordiness means you are using too
 many words to convey your meaning. The general
 guideline here is that if you can use one word or many
 words to convey your meaning, always use the one word.
• One of the most common is the use of the phrase the fact
 that as in due to the fact that. Due to the fact that can be
 replaced with because. Other constructions using the fact
 that it is easier to just drop the phrase altogether.

Wordiness Cont’d


• Another example of a wordy construction is a[the] something by the[of].
 Examples of this include a person by the name of Bob, the area of Tongshan, the
 element of aluminum. It is more concise and clearer if you just write Bob, Tongshan
 or aluminum.
• Wordy Concise
• At all times Always
• At the present time Now
• At this point in time Now
• For the purpose of For
• Due to the fact that Because
• The reason for this is Because
• Has not occurred Yet
• From that time until now Since

Redundancy


• Avoid redundancy. Redundancy refers to the unnecessary
 repeating of information that the reader already knows,
 explaining things that do not need to be explained or
 simply having a list of words that mean the same thing. It
 is much better to just state something once than to
 continually repeat, restate, reiterate and resay the same
 thing over and over again and again. (See how annoying
 it can be?)

Why being concise is important
• A lack of concision can make your writing dull, you
 seem pompous and your meaning can be lost.
 Consider the following sentence:
• “All things considered, in my opinion I think that
 due to the fact that we are currently in a recession,
 an economic downturn, at this point in history it is
 increasing likely that unskilled workers who have
 little or no job training in a given field of
 employment are finding it difficult, arduous and
 onerous to find gainful employment at livable
 wages sufficient to support themselves let alone a
 family during the present moment is our economic
 history due to the fact that the economy is
 experiencing negative growth.”

Importance Cont’d


• It is a word salad. What the student was trying to say was
 completely lost in a cascade of words. Now imagine
 reading four pages of writing like that. Here is the revised,
 concise sentence: “Because of the current recession,
 unskilled workers are having a difficult time finding
 employment at livable wages.”

On Clarity



• Clarity refers to using words and phrases to clearly state
 your meaning. There are a number of issues that go to
 clarity that will be discussed when we talk about
 sentences. What I want to deal with here is issues relating
 to poor word choice that can make your meaning difficult
 to understand.

the right word in the right form


• Make sure the words you are using mean what you think
 they mean.
• A dictionary is your friend; if you are not sure of a word,
 look it up (or ask me)
• Example One: After boarding the train, I walked down the
 isle to my seat. This makes no sense. Isle is the wrong
 word. Aisle would be the correct word.

Cont’d


• A thesaurus is not your friend.
• Stallion, mare, gelding, trotter, thoroughbred, Morgan,
 carter, cob and nag are all listed in a thesaurus under
 Horse but they all have slightly different meanings.
• Words in English also change their form depending on
 whether it is being used as an adjective, noun or verb.
 Always double-check if you are using the correct form.

Cont’d



• Nation is the noun referring to a country but national is
 the adjective form. To nationalize is a verb form of nation
 that means to bring something under control of the
 government.

Avoid obscure or archaic words

• While writers like Jane Austen and the Bronte sisters
 are fine to read they should not be taken as models for
 contemporary English usage. If you use their style of
 writing as a model you will not only come across as
 being overly formal and pretentious but you will also
 confuse your readers. Sentences like “We wended
 home to our palace of pulchritude” would serve only to
 confuse a reader. Wended and pulchritude are no longer
 current. A better, more modern version would be “We
 went home to our beautiful house.”
• The most common archaic usage is of as a replacement
 for because.

Cont’d

• Obscure usage covers a multitude of writing sins
 from slang, especially new slang, regional words and
 phrases, foreign words other than place and personal
 names used instead of their English versions, words
 that are uncommon and jargon when writing for a
 general audience.
• A dude was looking for the bubbler when he went
 through the foris to the biblioteca to discover catalog
 systems CPU interface.

Cont’d


• A good rule of thumb here is to always use a more familiar
 word to convey your meaning.
• The problem of jargon: All jargon means is technical language.
• If you are writing for someone who is in your field then
 technical language is entirely appropriate and should be used
 because it is most effective to convey your meaning. If,
 however, you are writing for a general audience then it should
 be used sparingly and if you do use it, then explain your terms.

• Avoid Culture-specific Idioms: Here I am referring to those
 expressions that are culturally specific. These expressions
 really cannot be directly translated because they will not
 be understood.

On Being Concrete

• Clear, concise writing in English requires a degree
 of concreteness—being specific and exact. The
 opposite of being concrete is being vague—
 inexact and ambiguous.
• General Words: General words are those that
 refer to categories or types of things rather than
 specific examples of them. Clothing, furniture,
 bird, wine, scenery and books are general words
 that can be replaced with more specific ones like
 shirt, chair, oriole, merlot, mountains and novels.

More on General Words



• We can still do better: My blue, button-down shirt, the
 brown-leather easy chair in Professor Jones’ office, the
 oriole in the tree outside my window, a 1998 merlot from
 Gallo, the gently sloping mountains of Vermont and science
 fiction novels of H.G. Wells

Avoid Abstract Words


• An abstract word refers to ideas and concepts which are
 inherently vague. Words like beautiful, moral, justice,
 freedom, government and peace are inherently vague
 because they do not have an agreed upon definition.
• For effective student writing is better to explain what you
 mean by these terms or replace them, especially
 beautiful, with descriptions of what you mean exactly.

Comparison Words


• Words like tall, short, long, brief, big and small all speak to
 relative size.
• For reasons of clarity, context must be included.
• A person may be tall, short or average height depending
 on where he or she is. Thus someone is short in the United
 States but is average height in China and a giant among
 the Bushmen of the Kalahari. To just say the person is tall
 conveys no real meaning.

Evaluation Words



• Words like good, better, best, bad, worse and worst really
 do not convey much meaning other than you prefer one
 thing over another unless you explain why you think it is
 better or worse.

Why Being Concrete is Important


• One of the main purposes of writing is to convey exactly
 what you mean so that you may be understood when you
 are not there to answer questions. A vague sentence or
 passage that is vague or ambiguous simply leaves too
 much out. The scenery was beautiful. It is much better than
 at home.This pair of sentences tells a reader absolutely
 nothing.

Cont’d


• The mountains, with their quiet, tree-covered, gentled slopes,
 and clear fresh air, are more relaxing than the crowded, noisy,
 smog-filled streets of my home city.This one, concrete sentence
 is better than the first two because now a reader knows exactly
 what type of scenery is being discussed, why it may be
 considered beautiful. We also have a better understanding of
 why the scenery is “better.” Whenever a teacher told you to try
 to write complex sentences, what they really meant was to try
 to write a more concrete sentence.

Basic Structures- Sentences


• The English declarative sentence is the most common
 one used in writing particularly essays. (Avoid rhetorical
 questions as a matter of both style and logic).
• One sentence equals one thought.
• The first type is descriptive: Subject-verb-adjective. Here
 use only verbs relating to the five senses or the verb to be.
 The cat is black. The food smells horrible.

Cont’d



• The second, and most common, is the Subject-Verb-
 Object sentence. The most common error I see is the run-
 on sentence. When you get to the end of this structure
 STOP, put a period and begin your next sentence. Henry
 went to the store and I like ice cream. This is really two
 separate thoughts and should be separate sentences.

Sentence Subjects


• The subject of an English Declarative sentence is very
 important. It should be the person or thing responsible,
 who performs the action what the sentence is really
 about. In English we make a distinction between the true
 subject and the grammatical subject. Always try to make
 the true subject—the thing the sentence is really about
 your grammatical subject.

Subject Examples


• The star was seen by the astronomers. In English this is a
 horrible sentence. The grammatical subject is the star but the
 star isn’t really doing anything. The people actually doing
 something are the astronomers. Make them the grammatical
 subject. The astronomers saw the star.The second sentence is
 clearer, more concise and much more effective. If you don’t
 have the true subject as your grammatical you will be
 considered a weak writer unsure of your subject.
• The word by when not followed by a location is a good sign you
 have a subject problem.

Verbs and Objects.



• Verbs are the action of the sentence.
• Objects refer to the acted upon, the instruments, the
 goals or origins, reasons locations.
• John (subject) smashed (verb) the bug (acted upon) with a
 magazine (instrument) near the window (location)

Misc. Considerations


• Pay attention to functional words like prepositions
 and qualifiers. They can radically change the
 meaning of a sentence.
• Henry went to the store.
• Henry went from the store.
• Only coaches say athletes make the best students.
• Coaches only say athletes make the best students.
• Coaches say only athletes make the best students.

The Mother of All English Grammar
 Rules

• Keep words together that belong together.
• Any sort of descriptor—single adjectives, phrases, clauses
 MUST be next to the word they are describing.
• Blue I live in a house.
• As a single mother of a three-year-old girl who works full
 time and attends college I find I have little free time.
• Do not be afraid to write shorter sentences.

Paragraphs


• One paragraph equals one fully explained idea.
• A good paragraph contains one general sentence that is
 the idea of the paragraph. This is generally referred to as
 the topic sentence.
• All other sentences in a paragraph are very specific
 sentences that either explain or illustrate the topic
 sentence.
• In academic writing, paragraphs tend to be longer
 because here is where you present your evidence.

The Five Paragraph Essay



• Invented by the ancient Roman rhetorician Cicero.
• Originally intended to be a fall back, it has since come to
 be a standard form to constructing essays.
• It is easy to plug in any side of any question to fit this
 form.

The introduction



• Put the issue/topic in a larger context, include why it is
 important, and generally introduce your subject.
• End with a sentence that clearly states your position
 along with three reasons why you hold it.
• That last sentence is your thesis.

The Body



• In order, write a single paragraph for each of the reasons
 you just listed. Only use transition words or phrases at the
 beginning or end of each paragraph.
• These paragraphs should be specific. They should include
 examples, quotes (if research is required), definitions,
 descriptions or other very specific bits of evidence.

Cont’d


• For longer essays (two to four pages): keep only three
 reasons for your position but expand the body to include
 more examples.
• For long research papers: add an additional reasons and
 extend examples to cover almost all cases.
• For both types of long papers, think one or two paragraph
 breaks per page.

The Conclusion

• Summarize the main bits of evidence you used.
• Restate your thesis (reword it, don’t just copy it).
• Explain how the evidence supports each part of your thesis
 (the three reasons).
• A writer’s trick: if after writing your body and conclusion, you
 find your conclusion is other than your thesis-change your
 thesis.

Article Questions


• 1. What is Prothero’s thesis?
• 2. Where does each of his three sections of his body begin and
 end?
• 3. For section one, does Prothero’s evidence support that part
 of his thesis?
• 4. For section two, does Prothero’s evidence support that part
 of his thesis?
• 5. For section three, does Prothero’s evidence support that
 part of his thesis?

Perennial Philosophy


• 1. There is both a material and spiritual/divine aspect to the universe.
• 2. Human beings can know about the spiritual/divine nature of the
 universe.
• 3. Human beings have both a material and spiritual/divine nature.
• 4. It should be the goal of human beings to identify with their
 spiritual/divine natures. (Huxley 13)
• --Huxley, Aldous. Introduction. The Bhagavad-Gita Translated by
 Swami Prabhavananda and Christopher Isherwood. New York: Signet
 Classic, 1972 11-23.

What Prothero Did Well And What
 He Did Poorly

• He followed the overall structure well—a solid
 introduction ending with a clear thesis that governed the
 body.
• His evidence is valid—although not always the strongest.
 But his evidence in sections one and two seems to prove a
 different idea than the one presented in his thesis (untrue
 and disrespectful).
• His conclusion does not match his thesis, lacks a
 summary of his key evidence and does not connect that
 evidence to his thesis.

Writing an Essay: The Process

• Follow the guidelines below for better essays.
 Never, ever, ever write anything for submission to
 a class or publication only once.
• Step One: DO THE RESEARCH! Never begin to
 draft an essay of any length without knowledge
 of your subject. Never.
• Step Two: Group your gathered evidence into
 related sub-topics (make note of your sources).
 Here the method matters less than the actually
 action. Each of these sub-topics are going to be
 part of your thesis.

Cont’d


• Step Three: Ask yourself what you think the sub-topics
 mean—take a position.
• Step Four: Once you have your position/working thesis
 with the reasons or sub-topics, draft the essay.
• Step Five: Look at your conclusion as discussed earlier. If
 your conclusion matches your thesis, go to step six. If not,
 rewrite your THESIS into a new working thesis. (A very
 bad mistake here is to try to force your more thoughtful
 conclusion to fit your working thesis.)

Cont’d

• Step Six: Look again at your evidence in the body of your
 essay. Is your evidence valid? If not, go back to the library.
 Is your evidence current? If not find more recent evidence.
 Is your evidence complete? Lastly does it prove what you
 said it proved or does it prove something other than what
 you thought it proved? If it is other, rewrite your THESIS.
 (The worst mistake is trying to force the evidence)

Cont’d



• Step Seven: Rewrite your essay based on the NEW thesis
 following the structure.
• Step Eight: Proof-read (also called editing). Fix any
 grammar or usage problems.
• Step Nine: Print and submit.

Sources and Evidence/Types


• Personal Experience/Observation. This is evidence based
 on examples from your own experience—either things
 that happened to you, someone you know or something
 you have seen. When using this type of evidence be
 careful not to form hasty conclusions.
• Analogy. This is a form of comparison where you use
 parallel cases to prove something about your topic by
 comparing it to a similar case. Beware the false analogy.

Continued/Evidence and
 Sources/Types


• Authority—Anything you look up on-line, in books or
 journals.
• Credibility of Sources—is the writer an expert? How does
 she handle the evidence? Is his evidence complete? Does
 the writer exhibit bias?
• A good rule of thumb: never rely on a single source.

Other Forms of Evidence





Experiment/survey research/observation: Depending on
your field, these may be used as well. Each field has its own
standards that must be adhered to but there are some
common features: details of the conditions, the “raw data”
must be kept and a discussion of the methodologies need to
be used.

Source Citation


• In research/essay writing, citing your sources is essential.
 Knowing when and what to have a source citation for
 protects you from allegations of plagiarism (theft of
 another’s work or ideas). Also, citations make clear what
 is your thoughts, ideas and interpretations of your
 evidence.
• Although there is an informal way to cite sources when
 writing for a general audience, we will keep to the
 academic standard for this class.

What You Do Not Need to Cite


• No citation is need for YOUR thoughts and
 interpretations of the evidence, the results of your own
 observations and experiments (you do need to provide
 details like when and where you made your observations)
 your own descriptions of things.
• The conclusion of an academic work, including the
 summary of your evidence, is generally your work and
 does not need a citation.

What You Do Not Need to Cite


• The other big area that does not need a citation is what is
 called common knowledge for the topic you are writing
 about. If you are not sure if something is common knowledge
 or not check to see if your sources cite a given fact or not.
 When in doubt it is better to cite than not cite.
• Common knowledge usually refers to basic facts—dates of
 events, names of participants, geographic locations.

What You MUST Cite


• Every direct quote—when you directly copy from a
 source. These should be set off with quotation marks (for
 short quotes) or be an indented block for quotes that are
 four lines or more—must be cited.
• Every paraphrase—when you re-write information and
 ideas from a source using your own sentence structure
 and words—must be cited.

How to Cite


• Every discipline has its own format for the works cited
 page and the citations in the text.
• All of them include the same basic information, however.
• That information is author’s name, title of the source,
 publisher or journal, place of publication, date of
 publication, page you found the information

Two Examples (Fictional)



• Jones, Henry Jr., “Legends of the Ark”, Journal of Biblical
 Archeology, 20.6 (1936) 56-69.
• In the body of the text (Jones 58)
• Jones, Henry Jr. Mythical Relics of the Ancient Near East.
 Cambridge: Harvard UP, 1936.

Paraphrasing



• The original quote “[The Bevel-rimmed Bowl] travelled with
 Uruk civilization, an indicator of Sumerian influence across
 the region, but also a great archaeological clue as to how this
 civilization organized itself…. The BRB suggests that the first
 cities had a redistributive economy….” (Miles 9)

Cont’d



• A bad paraphrase: The Bevel-rimmed Bowl went with Uruk
 civilization, indicating Sumerian influence across the region,
 but also a great archaeological clue as to how this civilization
 organized itself. The BRB suggests that the first cities had a
 redistributive economy. (Miles 9)
• If you do not really change the structure of the quote—just
 keep the quote.

Cont’d



• A good paraphrase: One of the strongest indicators of both
 the extent of Sumerian ideas about civilization and suggestive
 of the type of economy of these early cities is the BRB. The
 BRB, which seems to have originated in Uruk, may indicate a
 redistributive economy because the theory is that the BRB
 was used to pay workers. (Miles 9)

Thoughts on the Thesis and
 Argumentation


• A good thesis should be as specific as possible—in both
 the subject and the reasons. The reasons should be
 topical. A bad thesis is overly broad and lacks those
 specific topical terms.

Cont’d

• Bad: The Fire and Water Café was my favorite place.
• Good: The Fire and Water Café was my favorite place
 because it had good, cheap coffee, provided a good place
 to write during the day and a variety of entertainment
 during the evening.
• A good thesis is clear and determines the sections of the
 body of the essay.

Cont’d


• There should be no part of your essay that does not
 address part of your thesis.
• The very first thing about the body is that it should follow
 the thesis.
• Good argumentation, in the body of your essay, is about
 evidence and connecting that evidence back to what you
 are trying to prove.

From Interest to Essay


• No essay ever starts with a working thesis.
• Rather, they start with a writer having a question or
 wanting to find out more about an issue or subject.
• Helpful hint: Never pick a topic because you think a
 teacher will be interested in it—pick one YOU are
 interested in.
• Tell me about an historical event you are interested in.

Narrowing a Topic


• Once you have a general topic, you need to narrow it down to
 something that is doable in the length you have to write.
• Many students try to cover too big of a topic for the paper
 length they have been assigned.
• Continue to ask yourself what is it about the topic that
 interests you. Continue to do that until you have something
 specific enough to cover clearly, concisely and concretely in
 the length you have to work with.

Your Assignment


• Write a five-paragraph essay on a topic of your
 choosing—it can either be a persuasive essay or a topical
 one.
• This will be an annotated essay with at least two sources.
• A few tips—This is a short essay; pick your best evidence
 for each of your body paragraphs. Pick something you are
 interested in and can be reasonable about.
